steps: Statement II: branching decreases the boiling point, e.g. butan-1-ol > 2-methylpropan-2-ol → false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', physical properties (boiling points)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Ethanoic acid reacts with chlorine in the presence of a small amount of red phosphorus to give chloroethanoic acid. This reaction is known as the:

solution.explanation: Carboxylic acids with an α-hydrogen are halogenated at the α-carbon by Cl₂ or Br₂ with a little red phosphorus; this is the Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction.
solution.why_others_wrong: The Kolbe reaction makes salicylic acid from phenoxide and CO₂. Rosenmund reduction turns acyl chlorides into aldehydes. The Etard reaction oxidises toluene to benzaldehyde.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', reactions of carboxylic acids (HVZ reaction)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the common name in List-I with the IUPAC name in List-II.

List-I:
A. Catechol
B. Resorcinol
C. Quinol (hydroquinone)
D. o-Cresol

List-II:
I. Benzene-1,4-diol
II. 2-Methylphenol
III. Benzene-1,2-diol
IV. Benzene-1,3-diol

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT gives the common names of the dihydroxybenzenes and the methylphenols (cresols).
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV, B-III swaps catechol and resorcinol. B-I, C-IV swaps resorcinol and quinol. A-I, C-III swaps catechol and quinol.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', nomenclature (phenols)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 3.7 g of a saturated monocarboxylic acid reacts completely with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution and liberates 1.12 L of CO₂ measured at STP. The acid is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16; molar volume = 22.4 L mol⁻¹):

solution.concept: Molar mass of an acid from CO₂ evolved with NaHCO₃
solution.explanation: RCOOH + NaHCO₃ → RCOONa + H₂O + CO₂: one mole of a monocarboxylic acid gives one mole of CO₂.
solution.why_others_wrong: Methanoic (46), ethanoic (60) and butanoic (88 g mol⁻¹) acids do not have molar mass 74; taking two CO₂ per acid would give 148, which matches none of them either.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', reactions of carboxylic acids with hydrogencarbonates

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 8.8 g of ethanal is converted completely by dilute NaOH into the aldol, 3-hydroxybutanal. The mass of aldol formed is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16):

solution.explanation: Two molecules of ethanal combine without losing any atoms: 2CH₃CHO → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO. The mass is therefore conserved.
solution.why_others_wrong: 17.6 g takes one aldol per ethanal. 4.4 g halves the mass. 7.0 g is the mass of but-2-enal, formed only if the aldol is dehydrated on heating.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', aldol condensation

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Phenol is treated with bromine in carbon disulphide (CS₂) at low temperature. The main product is:

options.text: A mixture of o-bromophenol and p-bromophenol

solution.concept: Effect of solvent on bromination of phenol
solution.explanation: In a solvent of low polarity such as CS₂ or CHCl₃ at low temperature, phenol gives monobromophenols. With bromine water, the ring is so strongly activated that 2,4,6-tribromophenol is formed.
steps: Low polarity solvent, low temperature → monosubstitution
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,4,6-Tribromophenol forms with bromine water. –OH does not direct meta. The C–O bond of phenol is not replaced by bromine.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', electrophilic substitution in phenols (halogenation)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A mixture of o-bromophenol and p-bromophenol

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones in nucleophilic addition reactions.
Reason (R): The +I effect of the two alkyl groups in a ketone increases the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Relative reactivity of aldehydes and ketones
solution.explanation: Two alkyl groups in a ketone hinder the approach of the nucleophile (steric effect) and, by their +I effect, reduce the positive character of the carbonyl carbon. Both effects make ketones less reactive.
steps: A: e.g. ethanal reacts faster than propanone → true
R: the +I effect decreases, not increases, the electrophilicity → false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', nucleophilic addition (reactivity)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about ethers are correct?

(a) The alkoxy group of anisole directs electrophiles to the ortho and para positions.
(b) Anisole reacts with bromine in ethanoic acid, even without FeBr₃, to give mainly p-bromoanisole.
(c) Methyl tert-butyl ether reacts with HI to give methanol and tert-butyl iodide.
(d) Williamson synthesis with a tertiary alkyl halide and sodium methoxide gives a good yield of the ether.
(e) Diethyl ether reacts with sodium metal to liberate hydrogen.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: The –OR group activates the ring and directs o/p. With HI, a tertiary alkyl group leaves as a stable carbocation (SN1), so iodide ends up on the tertiary carbon. A tertiary halide with an alkoxide undergoes elimination. Ethers have no O–H bond, so sodium does not react.
steps: (b) p-bromoanisole is the main product → true
(d) The alkoxide acts as a base; the alkene is formed → false
(e) No acidic hydrogen → no reaction with Na → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option contains (d) or (e), or leaves out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', preparation and chemical reactions of ethers

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Each compound in List-I is treated with CH₃MgBr and the product is hydrolysed. Match it with the final organic product in List-II.

List-I:
A. CH₃CHO
B. HCHO
C. CH₃COCH₃
D. CO₂

List-II:
I. Ethanoic acid
II. 2-Methylpropan-2-ol
III. Ethanol
IV. Propan-2-ol

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Grignard reagents with carbonyl compounds and CO₂
solution.explanation: CH₃⁻ of the Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon. Methanal gives a primary alcohol, other aldehydes secondary alcohols, ketones tertiary alcohols, and CO₂ a carboxylic acid.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-III, B-IV swaps the products of ethanal and methanal. C-I, D-II gives the acid to the ketone. A-II, C-IV swaps the secondary and tertiary alcohols.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', preparation of alcohols from Grignard reagents; Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', preparation of carboxylic acids
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Electron-donating groups increase the acidity of carboxylic acids.
Statement II: Benzoic acid is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Effect of substituents on acidity of carboxylic acids
solution.explanation: Electron-withdrawing groups stabilise the carboxylate anion and increase acidity; electron-donating groups destabilise it and decrease acidity. Benzoic acid (pKa 4.19) is stronger than ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76).
steps: Statement I: electron-donating groups decrease acidity → false
Statement II: pKa 4.19 < 4.76 → benzoic acid is stronger → true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', acidity of carboxylic acids
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 0.37 g of a saturated monohydric alcohol reacts with excess methylmagnesium iodide and gives 112 mL of methane measured at STP. The molecular formula of the alcohol is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16; molar volume at STP = 22400 mL):

solution.concept: Molar mass from the reaction of an alcohol with a Grignard reagent
solution.explanation: A Grignard reagent takes the acidic hydrogen of the –OH group: ROH + CH₃MgI → CH₄ + Mg(OR)I. One mole of a monohydric alcohol gives one mole of methane.
solution.why_others_wrong: C₃H₈O (60), C₅H₁₂O (88) and C₂H₆O (46 g mol⁻¹) do not have molar mass 74.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Haloalkanes and Haloarenes', Grignard reagents (reaction with proton sources)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 4.4 g of ethanal is converted into its cyanohydrin with HCN, and the cyanohydrin is hydrolysed completely with dilute acid to 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid). Assuming complete conversion in both steps, the mass of lactic acid formed is (C = 12, H = 1, N = 14, O = 16):

solution.explanation: HCN adds to C=O to give CH₃CH(OH)CN; acid hydrolysis converts –CN into –COOH. Each step is 1 : 1 in moles.
steps: CH₃CH(OH)CN (71 g mol⁻¹) → CH₃CH(OH)COOH (90 g mol⁻¹)
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.1 g is the mass of the cyanohydrin, before hydrolysis. 4.4 g assumes no change in mass. 18.0 g doubles the amount.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', nucleophilic addition of HCN; preparation of carboxylic acids from nitriles

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: An ester X (C₄H₈O₂) is hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid Y and an alcohol Z. Oxidation of Z with acidified dichromate gives Y. X is:

solution.concept: Identifying an ester from its hydrolysis products
solution.explanation: A primary alcohol is oxidised to the acid with the same number of carbon atoms. If Z gives Y, the acid and alcohol parts of the ester have the same carbon count, i.e. two carbons each in C₄H₈O₂.
solution.why_others_wrong: Methyl propanoate gives methanol, which oxidises to methanoic acid, not propanoic acid. Propyl methanoate gives propan-1-ol, which oxidises to propanoic acid, not methanoic acid. Isopropyl methanoate gives propan-2-ol, which oxidises to propanone.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', esters; oxidation of alcohols

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about aldol and related reactions are correct?

(a) Methanal and benzaldehyde cannot undergo aldol condensation by themselves.
(b) A cross aldol reaction between ethanal and propanal gives a mixture of four products.
(c) Ketones that have α-hydrogen atoms do not undergo aldol condensation.
(d) Benzaldehyde condenses with acetophenone in dilute alkali to give an α,β-unsaturated ketone (Claisen–Schmidt condensation).
(e) Aldehydes that have α-hydrogen atoms undergo the Cannizzaro reaction with concentrated alkali.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Aldol, cross aldol and Cannizzaro reactions
solution.explanation: Aldol condensation needs at least one α-hydrogen; aldehydes and ketones with α-H both react. With two different enolisable aldehydes, each can act as donor and acceptor, giving four products. Aldehydes without α-H undergo the Cannizzaro reaction.
steps: (a) HCHO and C₆H₅CHO have no α-H → true
(e) Cannizzaro is for aldehydes without α-H → false
solution.why_others_wrong: (a), (b) and (c) includes the false (c); the other options contain (c) or (e).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', aldol, cross aldol and Cannizzaro reactions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Propanal has a higher boiling point than propan-1-ol.
Reason (R): Aldehydes show dipole–dipole interactions but cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds as alcohols do.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Boiling points of aldehydes compared with alcohols
solution.explanation: Aldehydes and ketones boil higher than hydrocarbons and ethers of comparable mass (dipole–dipole forces) but lower than alcohols, which are associated through hydrogen bonds.
steps: A: propanal (b.p. about 322 K) boils below propan-1-ol (about 370 K) → false
R: no O–H bond in aldehydes → no intermolecular H-bonding → true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', physical properties
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Ethanenitrile, CH₃CN, is reduced with lithium aluminium hydride. The product is:

solution.explanation: Nitriles are reduced by LiAlH₄ (or by catalytic hydrogenation) to primary amines with the same number of carbon atoms: R–C≡N → R–CH₂–NH₂.
solution.why_others_wrong: Methanamine has one carbon fewer (that is a Hofmann-type result). Ethanamide is formed by partial hydrolysis, not reduction. A secondary amine is not formed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', preparation of amines (reduction of nitriles)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Freshly distilled aniline is colourless, but on storage it gradually becomes coloured. This is due to:

options.text: Absorption of moisture from the air
Polymerisation by light into a dye
Reaction with carbon dioxide of the air

solution.explanation: NCERT notes that pure amines are colourless, but aryl amines such as aniline become coloured on storage because of atmospheric oxidation.
steps: Aniline is easily oxidised; air slowly converts it into coloured products
solution.why_others_wrong: Moisture or CO₂ does not give coloured products, and the colour is not due to polymerisation into a dye.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', physical properties

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In the ammonolysis of an alkyl halide, the primary amine is obtained as the main product if a large excess of ammonia is used.
Statement II: The lower aliphatic amines are gases with a fishy odour.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: With excess ammonia, the alkyl halide is more likely to meet NH₃ than the amine already formed, so further alkylation is suppressed. NCERT describes the lower aliphatic amines as gases with a fishy odour.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', preparation (ammonolysis) and physical properties
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 9.3 g of aniline is acetylated completely with ethanoic anhydride. The mass of acetanilide formed is (C = 12, H = 1, N = 14, O = 16):

solution.explanation: C₆H₅NH₂ + (CH₃CO)₂O → C₆H₅NHCOCH₃ + CH₃COOH: one mole of aniline gives one mole of acetanilide.
steps: Molar mass of C₆H₅NHCOCH₃ = 135 g mol⁻¹
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.3 g ignores the added acetyl group. 6.75 g halves the amount and 27.0 g doubles it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', chemical reactions (acylation)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
How many of the following give the carbylamine (isocyanide) test?
CH₃NH₂, (CH₃)₂NH, C₆H₅NH₂, (CH₃)₃N, C₆H₅CH₂NH₂, C₆H₅NHCH₃

solution.explanation: Only primary amines (aliphatic or aromatic) give a foul-smelling isocyanide when heated with chloroform and ethanolic KOH. Secondary and tertiary amines do not.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 usually leaves out benzylamine, which is a primary amine. 4 wrongly includes N-methylaniline (secondary). 6 counts every amine.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', chemical reactions (carbylamine reaction)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Tertiary amines have higher boiling points than isomeric primary amines.
Reason (R): Tertiary amines have no hydrogen atom on nitrogen, so they cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Primary amines have two N–H hydrogens available for hydrogen bonding, secondary amines one and tertiary amines none. Hence the boiling points of isomeric amines follow primary > secondary > tertiary.
steps: A: tertiary amines boil lowest → false
R: no N–H → no intermolecular H-bonding → true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', physical properties (boiling points)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the method of preparing amines in List-I with its characteristic in List-II.

List-I:
A. Gabriel phthalimide synthesis
B. Hofmann bromamide degradation
C. Reduction of a nitrile
D. Ammonolysis of an alkyl halide

List-II:
I. Gives a mixture of 1°, 2° and 3° amines and a quaternary ammonium salt
II. Gives a primary amine with one carbon atom fewer than the amide
III. Gives only primary aliphatic amines; not used for aromatic amines
IV. Gives a primary amine with one carbon atom more than the alkyl halide used to make the nitrile

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Each method has a characteristic feature that NCERT highlights.
steps: Gabriel: 1° aliphatic only (aryl halides do not react with phthalimide anion) → III
Hofmann: RCONH₂ → RNH₂, one carbon lost → II
R–X → R–CN → R–CH₂NH₂: one carbon added (ascent of series) → IV
Ammonolysis: mixture of amines and quaternary salt → I
solution.why_others_wrong: A-II, B-III swaps the Gabriel and Hofmann methods. B-IV, C-II swaps the step-down and step-up methods. A-I, D-III swaps the Gabriel synthesis and ammonolysis.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', preparation of amines
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 0.59 g of a saturated aliphatic primary amine, CₙH₂ₙ₊₁NH₂, reacts completely with nitrous acid and liberates 224 mL of nitrogen measured at STP. The amine is (C = 12, H = 1, N = 14; molar volume at STP = 22400 mL):

solution.concept: Quantitative evolution of nitrogen from primary aliphatic amines
solution.explanation: Aliphatic primary amines react with nitrous acid through unstable diazonium salts, giving the alcohol and one mole of N₂ per mole of amine. NCERT notes that this quantitative evolution of N₂ is used in estimating amino acids and proteins.
solution.why_others_wrong: Methanamine (31), ethanamine (45) and butan-1-amine (73 g mol⁻¹) do not have molar mass 59.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', reaction with nitrous acid

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the weakest base?

solution.concept: Effect of ring substituents on the basicity of arylamines
solution.explanation: Electron-releasing groups such as –CH₃ increase the basic strength of aniline; electron-withdrawing groups such as –NO₂ decrease it. A p-nitro group withdraws the nitrogen lone pair by both −I and −R effects.
steps: p-NO₂: strongly withdraws electron density from –NH₂ → lone pair least available
p-CH₃ and N-CH₃: electron-releasing → slightly stronger bases than aniline
solution.why_others_wrong: Aniline is a stronger base than p-nitroaniline, and the methyl-substituted anilines are stronger still.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', basic character (arylamines)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about arenediazonium salts are correct?

(a) Benzenediazonium chloride is a colourless crystalline solid that is readily soluble in water.
(b) Benzenediazonium fluoroborate is insoluble in water and is stable at room temperature.
(c) Replacement of the diazo group by –Cl using CuCl/HCl is the Sandmeyer reaction.
(d) Diazotisation of aniline is carried out above 300 K for the best yield.
(e) Nitrogen is retained in the product in every reaction of diazonium salts.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Properties and reactions of diazonium salts
solution.explanation: Diazonium salts are prepared at 273–278 K because they decompose on warming. In most of their reactions N₂ is lost (replacement reactions); in coupling reactions nitrogen is retained.
steps: (e) Replacement reactions lose N₂; only coupling retains it → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Every option other than (a), (b) and (c) contains (d) or (e).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', diazonium salts (preparation, properties and reactions)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In proteins, the α-amino acids are joined by peptide linkages. A peptide linkage is:

solution.explanation: A peptide bond is an amide bond formed between the –COOH group of one amino acid and the –NH₂ group of another, with loss of a water molecule.
solution.why_others_wrong: –CO–O– is an ester linkage, –O– is the glycosidic (ether-type) linkage of carbohydrates, and –CH=N– is an imine.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', structure of proteins (peptide bond)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Amylose constitutes about what percentage of starch?

solution.explanation: Starch is a polymer of α-glucose made of two components: amylose (water soluble, about 15–20%) and amylopectin (water insoluble, about 80–85%).
steps: Amylose: unbranched, C1–C4 α-glycosidic links, 15–20% of starch
solution.why_others_wrong: 80–85% is the share of amylopectin. 50% and 98% are not the NCERT values.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', polysaccharides (starch)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How many peptide bonds are present in a linear pentapeptide?

solution.explanation: Each peptide bond joins two neighbouring amino acid residues, so a chain of n residues has n − 1 peptide bonds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 counts one bond per residue. 3 subtracts two. 10 counts all pairs of residues, not only neighbours.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', proteins (peptides)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 34.2 g of sucrose is hydrolysed completely with dilute acid. The mass of glucose formed is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16):

solution.explanation: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + C₆H₁₂O₆ (fructose). One mole of sucrose gives one mole of glucose and one mole of fructose.
solution.why_others_wrong: 36.0 g is the combined mass of glucose and fructose. 34.2 g assumes no change in mass. 9.0 g halves the amount of glucose.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', disaccharides (sucrose)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A dipeptide contains two peptide bonds.
Statement II: In nucleic acids, nucleotides are joined by glycosidic linkages between the sugar units.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Peptides and the nucleic acid backbone
solution.explanation: A dipeptide is formed from two amino acids joined by one peptide bond. In nucleic acids, nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester linkages between the 5′ and 3′ carbon atoms of the pentose sugars.
steps: Statement I: two residues → one peptide bond → false
Statement II: the linkage is a phosphodiester, not a glycosidic linkage → false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', proteins; structure of nucleic acids
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the level of protein structure in List-I with its description in List-II.

List-I:
A. Primary structure
B. Secondary structure
C. Tertiary structure
D. Quaternary structure

List-II:
I. α-helix and β-pleated sheet arrangements of the chain
II. Spatial arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits
III. Sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain
IV. Overall folding of the chain, giving fibrous or globular shapes

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT describes four levels. A change in the amino acid sequence changes the primary structure; hydrogen bonds within the backbone give the secondary structure; further folding gives the tertiary structure; association of subunits gives the quaternary structure.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-I, B-III swaps the primary and secondary levels. C-II, D-IV swaps the tertiary and quaternary levels. B-IV, C-I swaps the secondary and tertiary levels.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', structure of proteins
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Vitamin C must be supplied regularly in the diet.
Reason (R): Water-soluble vitamins are readily excreted in urine and cannot be stored in the body (vitamin B₁₂ excepted).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Vitamin C is water soluble. Because such vitamins are not stored and are lost in urine, a regular intake is needed.
steps: Vitamin C belongs to this group → R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', vitamins (classification)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about amino acids are correct?

(a) Amino acids are classified as acidic, basic or neutral according to the relative numbers of amino and carboxyl groups in their molecules.
(b) Lysine, which has two amino groups and one carboxyl group, is a basic amino acid.
(c) Amino acids are usually colourless, crystalline, high-melting solids.
(d) Amino acids that can be synthesised in the body are called essential amino acids.
(e) Proteins are polymers of β-amino acids.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Classification and properties of amino acids
solution.explanation: Amino acids exist as zwitterions and so behave like salts (high melting, crystalline). Those that the body can make are non-essential; those that must come from the diet are essential. Proteins are made of α-amino acids.
steps: (b) More amino than carboxyl groups → basic → true
(d) These are the non-essential amino acids → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Every option other than (a), (b) and (c) contains (d) or (e).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', amino acids (classification and properties)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How many chiral (asymmetric) carbon atoms are present in the six-membered cyclic (pyranose) form of α-D-glucose?

solution.concept: Chiral centres in the cyclic form of glucose
solution.explanation: Open-chain glucose has four chiral carbons (C2–C5). On ring formation, the –OH at C5 adds to the C1 aldehyde group, and C1 becomes a new chiral centre (the anomeric carbon).
steps: C1: H, OH, ring O, C2 → chiral (anomeric)
C2, C3, C4: chiral as in the open chain
C5: H, ring O, C4, CH₂OH → chiral
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 is the count for the open-chain form. 6 wrongly includes the CH₂OH carbon. 3 leaves out C1 and one more centre.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', cyclic structure of glucose (anomers)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar because:

options.text: It is a disaccharide with a molar mass greater than that of glucose
It contains a fructose unit, and ketoses can never reduce Fehling's solution
Its glucose unit has no free –OH groups
The reducing groups of both glucose (C1) and fructose (C2) are used up in the glycosidic bond

solution.explanation: A sugar reduces Fehling's or Tollens' reagent when it has a free aldehydic or ketonic group (a free anomeric carbon). In sucrose, C1 of α-D-glucose is joined to C2 of β-D-fructose, so neither unit has a free reducing group.
steps: Sucrose: α-D-glucose C1 – O – C2 β-D-fructose
Both anomeric carbons are tied up → non-reducing
Maltose and lactose keep one free anomeric carbon → reducing
solution.why_others_wrong: Molar mass has nothing to do with reducing power. Fructose itself is a reducing sugar. The glucose unit of sucrose still has free –OH groups at C2, C3, C4 and C6.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', disaccharides (sucrose)
solution.final_answer: Option D: The reducing groups of both glucose (C1) and fructose (C2) are used up in the glycosidic bond

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A salt is heated with sodium hydroxide solution. The gas evolved gives a brown precipitate with Nessler's reagent. The salt contains:

solution.concept: Test for the ammonium ion (group zero)
solution.explanation: Ammonium salts give ammonia gas when warmed with NaOH. Ammonia forms a brown precipitate with Nessler's reagent (alkaline K₂HgI₄).
solution.why_others_wrong: Na⁺, Ca²⁺ and Zn²⁺ do not release any gas when warmed with NaOH.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), qualitative analysis (test for NH₄⁺, group zero)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In the flame test, a salt imparts an apple-green (grassy green) colour to the flame. The cation present is:

solution.concept: Flame test for group V cations
solution.explanation: Volatile chlorides of some metals give characteristic flame colours: barium apple green, calcium brick red, strontium crimson red, potassium lilac (violet).
solution.why_others_wrong: Calcium gives brick red, strontium crimson red and potassium lilac.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), qualitative analysis (flame test, group V)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In titrations with potassium permanganate, the solution is acidified with dilute sulphuric acid.
Statement II: Nitric acid is preferred to sulphuric acid for acidifying permanganate titrations, because it is itself an oxidising agent.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Choice of acid in permanganate titrations
solution.explanation: The acid used must not react with permanganate or with the substance titrated. Dilute H₂SO₄ is stable towards both. Nitric acid is avoided precisely because it is an oxidising agent and would oxidise the reducing agent being estimated.
steps: Statement I: dilute H₂SO₄ is used → true
Statement II: HNO₃ is not used, because its own oxidising action would give a wrong titre → false
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), titrimetric analysis (redox titrations with KMnO₄)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In a study of the effect of temperature on the reaction between sodium thiosulphate and hydrochloric acid, the cross under the flask disappears after 80 s at 293 K. Assuming the rate doubles for every 10 K rise and that the time is inversely proportional to the rate, the time at 313 K (all concentrations unchanged) will be:

solution.concept: Effect of temperature on reaction rate
solution.explanation: A 20 K rise is two 10 K steps, so the rate becomes 2 × 2 = 4 times; the time becomes one quarter.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 s doubles the rate only once. 10 s uses a factor of 8 (three steps). 160 s makes the time longer, as if the rate fell with temperature.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), chemical kinetics (effect of temperature on the rate of reaction of thiosulphate with HCl)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Potash alum, K₂SO₄·Al₂(SO₄)₃·24H₂O, is prepared from aluminium sulphate and potassium sulphate. The maximum mass of potash alum that can be obtained from 3.42 g of anhydrous Al₂(SO₄)₃ is (K = 39, Al = 27, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1):

solution.concept: Stoichiometry of the preparation of potash alum
solution.explanation: One mole of Al₂(SO₄)₃ is present in one formula unit K₂SO₄·Al₂(SO₄)₃·24H₂O (molar mass 948 g mol⁻¹).
steps: Molar mass of Al₂(SO₄)₃ = 54 + 96 + 192 = 342 g mol⁻¹ → n = 3.42/342 = 0.01 mol
Molar mass of the alum = 174 + 342 + 432 = 948 g mol⁻¹
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.74 g uses the formula KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O (474) with a 1 : 1 ratio, forgetting that each Al₂(SO₄)₃ gives two such units. 18.96 g doubles the answer. 3.42 g ignores the added K₂SO₄ and water.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), preparation of inorganic compounds (potash alum)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.subtopic: Detection of elements and functional groups
questions.question_text:
Match the functional group in List-I with an observation that detects it in List-II.

List-I:
A. Carbon–carbon double bond
B. Alcoholic –OH
C. Carboxyl group
D. Aldehyde group

List-II:
I. Silver mirror with Tollens' reagent
II. Brisk effervescence with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution
III. Decolourisation of bromine water
IV. Red colour with ceric ammonium nitrate

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Each functional group has a characteristic laboratory test.
steps: C=C → adds bromine → bromine water decolourised → III
Alcohol → ceric ammonium nitrate turns from yellow to red → IV
–CHO → Tollens' reagent reduced to silver → I
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV, B-III swaps the tests for unsaturation and alcohols. C-I, D-II swaps the acid and aldehyde tests. B-II, C-IV gives the effervescence to the alcohol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In salt analysis, group II cations are precipitated as sulphides by H₂S in the presence of dilute HCl, whereas group IV cations are not precipitated under these conditions.
Reason (R): Dilute HCl increases the ionisation of H₂S, raising the sulphide ion concentration.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Role of HCl in group II precipitation
solution.explanation: H⁺ from HCl suppresses the ionisation of H₂S (common ion effect), so the S²⁻ concentration is low. Only the sulphides of very low solubility product (group II) exceed their Ksp; group IV sulphides need the higher S²⁻ concentration available in ammoniacal solution.
steps: R: HCl decreases, not increases, the ionisation of H₂S → false
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), systematic qualitative analysis of cations; Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', common ion effect
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 0.53 g of an impure sample of sodium carbonate is dissolved in water and titrated with 0.1 M HCl using methyl orange as indicator. 80.0 mL of the acid is needed. Assuming the impurities do not react, the percentage purity of the sample is (Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16):

solution.concept: Percentage purity from an acid–base titration
solution.explanation: With methyl orange the end point corresponds to complete neutralisation: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40% takes a 1 : 1 ratio of HCl to Na₂CO₃. 20% takes four HCl per Na₂CO₃. 42.4% reports the mass of pure carbonate (0.424 g) as if it were a percentage.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), titrimetric analysis (acid–base titrations)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following tests for anions are correctly described?

(a) Sulphate: a white precipitate with BaCl₂ solution that is insoluble in concentrated HCl or HNO₃.
(b) Acetate: a deep red colour with neutral iron(III) chloride solution.
(c) Sulphite: warming with dilute H₂SO₄ gives H₂S, which turns lead acetate paper black.
(d) Oxalate: decolourises warm, acidified KMnO₄ solution with evolution of CO₂.
(e) Nitrate: brown fumes of NO₂ with dilute H₂SO₄ in the cold.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Dilute H₂SO₄ releases SO₂ (not H₂S) from sulphites; SO₂ turns acidified dichromate paper green. Brown fumes with dilute acid are given by nitrite; nitrate needs concentrated H₂SO₄ (with copper turnings) or the brown ring test.
steps: (a) BaSO₄ is insoluble in acids → true
(b) Iron(III) acetate gives a deep red colour → true
(d) Oxalate is oxidised to CO₂ by MnO₄⁻ → true
(e) Nitrate does not give NO₂ with dilute acid → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option contains (c) or (e), or leaves out the true statement (d).
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), qualitative analysis (tests for anions)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The enthalpy of neutralisation of ethanoic acid by sodium hydroxide is less negative than that of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide.
Statement II: The enthalpy of solution of every salt in water is negative, so a salt always warms the water when it dissolves.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Enthalpy changes measured in the laboratory
solution.explanation: Part of the heat released when a weak acid is neutralised is used to complete its ionisation, so the enthalpy of neutralisation is less negative than about −57 kJ mol⁻¹. Many salts (e.g. KNO₃, NH₄Cl) dissolve endothermically and cool the water.
steps: Statement I: weak acid → energy used for ionisation → less heat released → true
Statement II: enthalpy of solution can be positive (KNO₃, NH₄Cl) → false
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), thermochemistry (enthalpy of solution and of neutralisation)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
